en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Bīlíng during the Táng Dynasty, this is a private arrangement of sixteen sets of questions and answers from the *Zhōngdū*. The first set of questions and answers asks generally why, among all objects of cognition, there are only ten;
for example, within the "entry into the aggregates" (*skandha-praveśa*), the various aggregates are not the same. [The text continues with] afflictions...
The distinctions among the types of afflictions are likewise immeasurable,
as are the various diseases, karmic actions, and even the provisional practices and correct conduct of the two vehicles within the two teachings,
as well as the differing stages of the bodhisattvas within the three teachings.
Therefore it is said: "If dharmas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, how can the objects be fixed at ten?
The intended meaning of the answer is indeed as you have asked:
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like the earth, and the seeds are like the objects.
Contemplative practice is like rain falling and sprouts emerging.
Briefly summarized by numerical methods, it reaches ten stages.
Next, following the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*), there are nine questions and answers.
This is for the purpose of establishing the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) of both the general and the specific.
First, the general question is raised;
second, in the response, the general permutation is answered first.
The text itself constitutes ten [sections].
Regarding the first, the meaning of the "aggregate" (*skandha*) as an object also applies to all ten;
however, based on two specific meanings, the aggregate must necessarily occupy the first position.
Although the subsequent text states that [the practice] specifically begins with the head,
the meaning of the present passage follows the general approach;
practitioners generally take the aggregates (skandhas) as the starting point for the body.
All sūtras generally take the aggregates (skandhas) as the starting point for contemplation.
Since the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) comes first, it is said that all sūtras begin with form.
This applies not only to the aggregates, but extends throughout the ten [bases].
Up to and including the meaning of "bodhisattva," these all apply across the ten [categories].
Within this context, although they are said to be "common" (*sāmānya*) based on their names, their meanings remain distinct.
For example, while the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) are commonly designated as the aggregates (*skandha*).
Yet, because they differ in terms of cause and effect, as well as in their distinct aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth,
their meanings are fundamentally different. Since this is the case for both the aggregates and their objects, [the same applies here].
The same applies to the other nine.
As for the initial general designation of "aggregate" (*skandha*),
it takes the aggregate as its fundamental objective sphere (*ālambana*).
Afflictions and karma are called the causes of the aggregates;
illness is the affliction of the aggregates;
and Māra is the master of the aggregates.
It is because one does not wish to cause others to exit the triple world.
Dhyāna constitutes a wholesome aggregate (skandha).
Furthermore, in relation to the ten objects, dhyāna constitutes a wholesome aggregate.
If discussed generally, the six persons,
the four [applications of mindfulness], and even the stages of subduing through various teachings such as the foundations of mindfulness,
are all subsumed within the aggregate of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-skandha*).
Now, because the two vehicles treat the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as distinct, they do not rely on the universal [definition].
Furthermore, the names of the objects of view and pride are also the causes of the aggregates;
the meaning of "cause" is the same as before, though it is listed later in the text.
Therefore, it is said "moreover.
Although the practitioners of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas have not yet transcended the realm,
in principle they differ from those in birth-and-death (saṃsāra) because their internal and external states are distinct.
It is called "distinct" because it differs from the previous eight.
Furthermore, if this object arises,
it is called "distinct" because it is subsumed under the aggregates (skandhas) of a realm outside [one's own].
Although these ten meanings differ, they collectively do not transcend the aggregates (*skandha*).
Because the specific is subsumed under the general, the general term "aggregate" is applied.
The inclusion of the nine objects within the general category of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) follows the same principle.
Regarding "dhyāna is immovable and so forth":
it is called "immovable" because it is the opposite of the movement of the desire realm.
Regarding "karma functions as affliction": [it means that karma serves as the activity of the afflictions].
If afflictions were without karma, they would lack the function of leading to future results.
To explain this point regarding the continuity of immovable karma,
the text states that karma is the function of afflictions.

The meaning of the text is that dhyāna is, in its essential function, the activity of the afflictions (*kleśa*); although it belongs to the realms of existence (*dhātu-bandhana*), it possesses the function of experiencing pleasure for a long duration, and is thus called "activity.
As for the statement that Māra governs the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth:
Although they preside over the desire realm with the intent to cause people to increase their fetters within the three realms,
both Śakra and Brahmā possess authority as rulers;
yet both are disciples of the Buddha who have grown weary of birth and death.
Therefore, it cannot be called the "lord of afflictions.
As for what are termed "distinctive afflictions," although they give rise to supramundane states of mind, these afflictions differ from the preceding seven.
Therefore, it is called "distinct.
This is a judgment based on the cause.
If judged from the perspective of the fruit:
The first seven possess both general and specific afflictions;
the latter two possess only specific afflictions.
While the meaning applies to both cause and effect, the intent of the text follows the cause.
Furthermore, from among those who have attained the fruit, one must further distinguish three types of bodhisattvas.
For example, even a bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka lineage who has not yet destroyed the pervasive afflictions is also termed "distinct" (pṛthagjana).
Therefore, the first interpretation should be taken as correct. Regarding the statement,
"The King’s illness is now grave," King Ajātaśatru intended for the sores on his body to be considered the illness.
The Tathāgata Jīvaka regards parricide as a transgression.
He asked:
"King Ajātaśatru has committed only one transgression, that of harming his father."
Why is it said that there are five? Answer:
Because they are subsumed within five categories, they are collectively referred to as "five."
Since the perverse is itself karma, karma is also called illness.
As for Māra being able to cause illness,
Māra does not afflict the physical body, its retribution, or the life-force.
They merely envy those who possess the Way and transform its people;
now, as for what they say regarding illness,
they hope that by means of physical sickness one will retreat from the path to Bodhi.
The three calamities are external illnesses; this clarifies that even meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is called an illness.
"Calamity" (*āpad*) is a specific synonym for "illness.
As the *Hongfan Wuxing* (The Great Plan: Five Elements) states:
Generally, whatever is harmful is termed a "calamity" (zāi).
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu zhuan) states:
"When Heaven reverses the seasons, it constitutes a calamity."
Furthermore, the conventions of traditional transmission state:
"A fire from heaven is called a *zai* (calamity).
Although this explanation exists, one truly does not know where heaven is located or the precise extent of such a calamity.
Therefore, one knows that this is not what is discussed by the Confucian masters.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"It requires seven fires and one water; after seven cycles of fire and water, there is wind."
After seven calamities of fire, there is one calamity of water.
In this manner, after seven cycles of seven calamities of fire and seven cycles of seven calamities of water,
there is yet another succession of seven calamities of fire.
First there is one wind calamity;
then, totaling eight, seven, five, and six fire calamities, followed by another seven fire calamities and one wind calamity. Why is it so?
Fire reaches the first dhyāna, water reaches the second dhyāna, and wind reaches the third dhyāna.
When the second dhyāna is destroyed, the first dhyāna is necessarily destroyed;
when the third dhyāna is destroyed, both the first and second are necessarily destroyed.
Therefore, in every kalpa, the first dhyāna is destroyed.
Because it accords with the one-kalpa lifespan of the first dhyāna,
one must pass through eight kalpas before reaching the second dhyāna.
In order to accord with the lifespan of eight kalpas in the third heaven of the second dhyāna,
the wind disaster must necessarily pass through sixty-four kalpas before reaching the third dhyāna;
this is to accord with the lifespan in the third heaven of the third dhyāna.
Therefore, in the first dhyāna, the internal affliction is vitarka and vicāra, while the external calamity is the fire disaster;
in the second dhyāna, the internal affliction is joy, while the external calamity is the water disaster;
in the third dhyāna, the internal affliction is pleasure, while the external calamity is the wind disaster.
Because the fourth dhyāna is free from affliction (*ādīnava*), it is likewise free from calamity (*upadrava*).
As for the present mention of "breathing, joy,
and bliss," this is in contrast to the fourth dhyāna, which is without breathing.
The lower three dhyānas possess inhalation, exhalation, and so forth;
the text omits vitarka and vicāra and speaks briefly only of joy and bliss.
Those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas are those who have "emptiness" as their illness.
Since these three types of bodhisattvas have not yet seen the Middle Way,
they share the same "sickness of emptiness" as the two vehicles.
As for the statement that "the sickness of emptiness is also empty":
Citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* as proof:
because emptiness itself is the sickness, it is called "the sickness of emptiness";
because that sickness of emptiness must itself be emptied, it is said to be "also empty."
This is because "emptiness within emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) is empty of "partial emptiness" (prādeśika-śūnyatā);
hence it is said that "it is also empty.
As for the statement, "afflictions, views, and pride are the root of karma":
This refers to the fundamental cause.
Based on these three, each is capable of performing its respective function.
This concerns the untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) of the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas.
This is also as previously distinguished.
As for those remaining which are subsumed under the demon of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha-māra*), the phenomena subsumed under formations are broad in scope.
Therefore, all other [defilements] are fully subsumed within it;
that is, they are subsumed under the māra of the aggregates (skandha-māra).
Afflictions, views, pride, and so forth are also termed "dhyāna" (meditative absorption).
Dhyāna is simply samādhi.
Since it also applies to mental factors (caitta), it possesses the name "samādhi.
Furthermore, this samādhi also extends to afflictions such as views and pride.
Therefore, these three are all termed "dhyāna.
As for Māra, he is one who has attained the fruit of the *anāgamya-samādhi*.
This stage of *anāgamya* may also be called "samādhi."
Having attained this concentration, one relinquishes the life-span and is reborn there; therefore, it is called the "fruit of concentration.
Regarding the pure dhyāna of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas, the Mahāyāna Sūtra (the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*) designates the four fundamental dhyānas as the "middle concentrations."
Therefore, this is now taken as pure dhyāna (*śuddha-dhyāna*).
Pure dhyāna is generally subsumed under the higher meditative absorptions (*ūrdhva-samādhi*).
For this reason, it will next be explained how these higher meditative absorptions encompass the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas.
The middle and lower concentrations encompass the remaining eight objects.
However, among the objects of dhyāna, only the fundamental states are subsumed under the middle concentration;
the *viśeṣa*, *abhijñā*, and *vidyā* should be subsumed under both categories.
The nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā) are subsumed under the higher meditative absorptions (ūrdhvadhyāna),
while the remaining seven objects are subsumed under the lower meditative absorptions (adhodhyāna).
As for what are called the "three absorptions" (tridhyāna):
Mahāvaipulya Sūtra, Fascicle 25:
"Good son, all sentient beings are fully endowed with the three concentrations."
This refers to the superior, the middling, and the inferior. The superior concentration refers to the Buddha-nature;
the middling concentration refers to all sentient beings being fully endowed with the first dhyāna.
Due to specific causes and conditions, one is able to cultivate it.
The lower concentration is subsumed under the mental factor of concentration within the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
However, the actual objects of the lower eight [meditations] belong to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Now, since the eight objects are expected to be associated with mental factors (*caitasika*), they generally possess the designation "concentrated" (*samāhita*).
Therefore, they are subsumed under the category of "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*) because these universal factors are associated with both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Although the sutra commentary states that the higher concentration belongs to the Buddha,
since it is stated that the middle concentration resides in the first dhyāna,
we now broadly designate both the two vehicles and bodhisattvas as possessing the higher concentration.
Regarding the inclusion of the view of self and the view of sentient beings within the aggregates (skandhas) and bases (āyatanas):
if discussed generally,
the sixteen types of knowledge and views are not separate from the aggregates and bases.
Now, because we speak from a specific perspective, the aggregates (*skandha*) taken collectively are called "sentient beings.
To conceptually impute a self (*ātman*) across these aggregates is called "the self.
That which is grasped and that which is imputed are termed the aggregates and sense bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding "afflictions possessing the five views":
as in the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the five views are fully present.
These ninety-eight are collectively termed afflictions.
Therefore, it is said that the afflictions subsume the five views.

Regarding the views of a "sick person," a "living being" (*jīva*), a "life-span" (*jīvita*), and a "person" (*pudgala*): "life-span" refers to the continuity [of existence], while "living being" refers to a single period [of life].
Ordinarily, although one considers the time of illness to be most urgent,
fearing that life may be cut short or that the continuity [of the path] will be severed,
one speaks from the perspective of what is more pressing; thus, it is contrasted with these two [other concerns].
Regarding those who hold views of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) concerning karma and dhyāna:
they conceive of a self that is capable of performing actions and practicing meditative concentration.
Therefore, they are called "agents" regarding dhyāna; they regard what is not the path to liberation as the path to liberation.
Therefore, it is called the clinging to precepts and observances. Māra, as the lord of desire, claims: "I am the one who drives them on; I am the agent. He claims:
"Suffering and pleasure arise from me; I am the experiencer."
It is so that in future lives they may still remain in the desire realm and be called "those who give rise to the proclivities" (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, birth and death are subsumed solely within the view of extremes;
birth and death are merely the beginning and end of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).
It is explained again as "also" (*yù*) because it belongs to the extremes (*anta*).
To conceive of birth as permanent and death as annihilated is why they are called "extremes."
As for the statement that pride is subsumed under the view of self:
because pride arises on account of the self,
pride belongs to the self.
Regarding those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas who are subsumed under "crooked views":
they are called "crooked" because their path is not the perfect, direct way.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
If one sees the Bodhisattva descend from Tuṣita, take a consort and procreate a son,
leave the city to renounce the world, and so forth until his final nirvāṇa,
this is called the crooked view of the two vehicles.
Although it is designated as the vehicle of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), it actually encompasses the path of teaching as well.
For example, manifesting a body for bodhisattvas prior to the stages is called the reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), not the self-enjoyment body (svasaṃbhogakāya),
because it is a provisional manifestation of another's body rather than a true [self-manifestation].
The meaning should be understood through the [following] verses.
These sixteen views are explained extensively in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom);
here, however, they are addressed only in relation to the eight.
Those not yet discussed are subsumed within the eight [categories].
That is to say, regarding "the one who gives birth," it refers to the view that calculates the one who produces sentient beings to be like parents giving birth to a child.
Second is the view of nurturing, which conceives that "I am able to nurture others.
Third is the view of enumeration,
which conceives that "I possess the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements."
The view of the four persons;
the view that conceives "I" as a practitioner;
and the view of the five appropriators.
First, calculating that one's future body shall receive the retribution;
second, the view that calculates that "I" am able to create the retribution of future lives.
The seventh is the view of those who know:
they reckon that the five faculties can cognize the five objects.
The eighth is the view of those who see.
The enumeration of the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and the ability to see forms, as well as the arising of false views,
is set forth in sequential order exactly as it appears in the sūtras, śāstras, and the *Dharmadhātuvyavasthāna*. Previously,
I cited these according to their meaning rather than following their sequential order.
If those who are outside the former eight [categories] were to be included within the former eight views,
then those who are born would be nurtured and brought under the domain of Māra;
although Māra is not identical to what the Brahmā King conceives him to be.
Those of similar affinity are collectively subsumed within the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Those who experience and those who initiate are subsumed within the realm of karma.
Those who are persons, knowers, and seers are subsumed within the sphere of afflictions.
As for being subsumed by the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and self-conceit (*asmimāna*): the grasping at "I" and "mine" is called self-conceit.
The *Abhidharmakośa* text is identical [in its phrasing]: "That which the aggregates (*skandha*) are, that is what I am able to conceive as 'I';
the afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves the conceit (*māna*), and the one who possesses them is the conceited person. The *Abhidharmakośa* says:
To consider oneself equal to others who are superior is called "overweening pride" (atimāna);
it has the same meaning as the affliction [of pride].
As for "pride of inferiority" (ūnamāna):
The treatise states:
To consider oneself slightly inferior when one is actually mostly superior is called "inferiority pride" (*ūnamāna*).
It is like a sick person who, though not as ill as others, still gives rise to pride.
Regarding those who are conceited about their karma and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
the treatise states:
"To regard that which is equal as being equal."
Although it is equal [to others], because the mind is loftily uplifted,
it is called pride (*māna*).
All those who attain meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) necessarily experience this self-elevation.
Therefore, self-conceit is called *mada*;
looking down upon others is called *māna*.
When Māra sees one who is greatly arrogant, he [seizes the opportunity].
The treatise states:
To consider oneself superior to one who is truly superior is called "conceit beyond conceit" (mānātimāna).
This refers to being conceited toward the Tathāgata, who is in fact superior even to a Buddha.
Regarding those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*),
the treatise states:
"To claim to have attained what one has not yet attained."
The stages of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas have not yet reached their ultimate limit;
when this object arises, they are unable to employ contemplation,
as it is precisely at the stage of predominance (*adhipati*).
Among the seven types of pride (*māna*), only false pride (*mithyāmāna*) is excluded.
This refers to claiming for oneself virtues that one does not possess when among people who do possess virtues;
it may also be included within the two objects of the demonic view (*mārādṛṣṭi*).
Because those two objects do not honor others,
they are collectively termed "within the Two Vehicles.
As for the inclusion of the nine objects within the Four Truths and the Four Foundations of Mindfulness:
Since the Four Truths of Dependent Origination are merely a sub-classification of the general Four Truths, it is somewhat more convenient to use the names and meanings of the latter;
therefore, one speaks only of the "Four Truths" rather than the "Four Truths of Dependent Origination.
Furthermore, the aggregates (skandhas) and bases (āyatanas) are entirely the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness.
This is the Truth of Suffering.
It is the entry point for the aggregates subsumed within the four foundations of mindfulness;
furthermore, it is distinguished by the specific nature of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the specific counterpart:
the patient is subsumed under the mindfulness of the body,
which likewise belongs to the Truth of Suffering.
Dhyāna is the mindfulness of dharmas; the mindfulness of sensations belongs to the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
Pure dhyāna is also subsumed under the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).
Among the mental sovereigns (citta-rāja) within the causal conditions of karma and habitual tendencies—namely, the dhyānas of afflictions, views, and pride—[this applies].
The mind-base (citta-smṛtyupasthāna) is subsumed under the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
All mental factors (caitasika), as well as the mental factors within the causal seeds of karma and habitual tendencies (vāsanā),
along with Māra and all phenomena (dharma), are subsumed under the truth of origination within the dharma-base (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna).
The bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is subsumed under the truths of the path and cessation.
This is because within the application of mindfulness to phenomena, the phenomena it encompasses are vast and manifold,
namely both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

If one discusses the objects of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) from the perspective of their inclusion within the aggregates (skandha), then the foundations of mindfulness do not include unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma). Therefore,
they are included only within the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) among the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, it is said that the four applications of mindfulness are subsumed within the four noble truths.

Furthermore, regarding the general correspondence: the objects of the applications of mindfulness are subsumed under the truth of suffering, while the wisdom that contemplates the applications of mindfulness is subsumed under the truth of the path.

In this way, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) encompass only the two objects of the aggregates (skandha) and sense bases (āyatana), as well as the four objects of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
Because they possess these many meanings, they are explained through both expansion and contraction.
Furthermore, if we consider them in terms of the nine foundations of mindfulness:
The first seven belong to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and are employed for the objects of the latter two;
if one includes the first eight, they should be explained as previously stated—
this can be seen by reflecting upon it.

Regarding the inclusion of the nine [categories] within the four great vows: since the Four Truths constitute the objective realm of the four great vows, they should be understood through the previous analysis.
As for the question regarding whether the names of the objective dharmas apply only generally: [the answer is as follows].
The four questions below all use specific points to challenge the general principle.
The intent of the first question is as follows:
since both objective phenomena and names mutually interpenetrate, [how can one distinguish between them?]
Can practitioners who are able to observe [the objects] also be included?
"Dharmas" refers to the ten objects in their essential nature;
"names" refers to the designations applied to those dharmas.
By means of these ten dharmas, one penetrates even that which has not yet transcended the aggregates,
up to and including what is collectively termed the dharma of a bodhisattva;
this is called the penetration of dharmas (dharmābhijñā).
The text states that [these terms] are general designations for the aggregates (skandha) and sense bases (āyatana), up to being general designations for the bodhisattva.
This constitutes the universality of names. Since the names of phenomena are thus universal, [the same applies to their nature].
Therefore, he asks again whether one who is able to practice is also "comprehensive" (tong).
The meaning of the answer is that it is precisely by being "both comprehensive" that the response is given.
Why is this? Because even before the preceding nine stages, when he has not yet generated the resolve for enlightenment,
he is still designated as a bodhisattva.
Therefore, while the objects of a bodhisattva’s sphere may extend to others,
for the sake of this text, nine objects are cited and collectively designated as "bodhisattva."
One should know that this also applies to practitioners.

As for the statement that those who have not yet generated the resolve are called "bodhisattvas," this is based on the principle that all sentient beings, by virtue of their inherent nature, shall all become Buddhas.
Is this not the case for a bodhisattva?
Question: The designation "object" (viṣaya) may be understood as being applicable broadly.
How is it that "dharma" is pervasive? Answer:
Since the name "dharma" designates all phenomena, its application is pervasive.
That Dharma is not partitioned;
when it is generally referred to as "the two vehicles" and so forth,
the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fa-hua lun) speaks of four kinds of śrāvakas.
This refers to those who abide in the fruits [of the path], those who manifest through transformation (*nirmāṇa*), those who regress from bodhi, and those with overweening pride (*abhimāna*).
Now, it is said that the Buddha-way is itself a manifestation through transformation.
As for the statement that "overweening pride subsumes the [remaining] eight [categories] below": [it means that these four categories encompass the other eight].
This is because the followers of the two vehicles are currently abiding in their respective fruits.
The objects discussed in this treatise that give rise to [cognition] are not the aforementioned eight objects;
furthermore, they do not share the same meaning as the bodhisattvas who abide in the fruit.
The regression from the bodhicitta is also included within the lower nine stages;
if one regresses to become a follower of the two vehicles,
then it is subsumed under the spheres of the two vehicles.
If one regresses from the perfect [vehicle] and enters the partial, it still belongs to the realm of the bodhisattva.
If both the Great and Small Vehicles are lost, then one falls into the lower eight stages.
Furthermore, within these dhyānas, one must distinguish between those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
One must examine this carefully in relation to the ten objects.
As for what is called the "Buddha-vehicle," it refers merely to the initial arousal of the mind and is by no means the ultimate perfection.
Next is a question and answer.
In the answer, the meaning is explained by means of a combined character;
that is, the specific meaning is used as the general name to serve as the response.
Regarding the initial question, "Is it that all are called 'common' (tong) because they are impermanent?"—
this asks whether the first ten objects (viṣaya), which both the two vehicles and bodhisattvas can attain, are termed "common," while the [remaining] eight,
which the three vehicles cannot attain, are termed "exclusive" (san-sheng).
Regarding the second point, "Are those which are not impermanent [themselves] impermanent?
the intended meaning of the answer is that the eight [categories] are not the Three Vehicles, yet they are fully subsumed within the Three Vehicles.
Second, it is not that there is no meaning of impermanence;
for this reason, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* cites that even outside the three realms there is still impermanence.
If even a bodhisattva is thus, [how much more so for others].
How much more so for those of the two vehicles?
Therefore, the latter two objects are both impermanent.
Next, the question and answer:
In the response, the meaning is explained by analyzing the words.
First, regarding the question of whether [the factors] are generally with outflows (*sāsrava*),
the previous eight points of difficulty are again applied to the latter two.
If it is admitted that impermanence is itself outflow (āsrava),
why was the *Ratnagotravibhāga* previously cited as stating that [the Buddha] "abides in the outflow-free realm" (*anāsravadhātu*)?
The intended meaning of the answer is as follows:
All that is pervasive is outflow (*āsrava*).
There is a view that they are not identical;
from the time after the Buddha’s descent [into the world] until now, all have been termed "outflows."
There is an interpretation that they differ because the ten objects are distinct;

the small lacks the characteristic of smallness, and the large lacks the characteristic of largeness;
these are of a different nature, and thus the large and the small do not interpenetrate one another.
If one says that "small" refers to the smallness of the large-and-small,
and "large" refers to the largeness of the small-and-large,
then these are termed the common nature of large and small, and they likewise do not interpenetrate.
If one says that "small" is not the smallness of small and large,
and "large" is not the largeness of large and small,
this is because there is no causal basis for small and large; therefore, they do not interpenetrate.
If one expresses principle through phenomena,
it is like the Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s analogy of a great thousand-fold world system scripture contained within a single speck of dust;
a single thought-moment is like such a minute particle.
The analogy of all phenomena being like a scroll of scripture,
and mustard seeds compared to Mount Sumeru, is likewise.
If one loses the intended meaning here, the underlying principle is truly difficult to reconcile.
From now on, "understanding and departing" refers precisely to the present family’s correct understanding:
it is simply that by acceding to the principle of the true suchness (tathatā) of the single thought-moment of the mind-nature, inconceivable functions arise.
Although in rationality there is no subject that perceives nor object perceived,
the subject and object appear distinct;
because one cultivates this principle, it is called "the practice of the capable."
Because one accords with this principle, it is called "being able to arrive.
Because of arriving, there is utility; this is explained in terms of realizing the principle.
Therefore, it is said that "the principle is superior to phenomena," though the wording here is abbreviated.
One should rely on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* for the explanation of the "Inconceivable" chapter (*Acintya-parivarta*).
The Sūtra says:
"Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called 'inconceivable' (*acintya*)."
If a bodhisattva dwells in this liberation,
they can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed;
even a single category is explained in this same manner.
Because the realization of liberation possesses inexhaustible functional utility,
it is said that even if one were to speak for an entire kalpa, one could not exhaustively describe it.
In the commentary (*shu*), this scriptural passage is explained solely by means of the three tracks (*san gui*).
There is no principle that is not fully exhausted.
The liberation of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is precisely the track of true nature (zhenxing gui).
It is also called "liberation through true nature.
If a bodhisattva abides in this liberation,
they then engage in contemplative observation.
It is also called the liberation through the wisdom of reality,
which is able to take the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru and immediately employ it as the means for accomplishment.
It is also called the pure liberation of skillful means.
The preceding text used the three teachings and three tracks of the former [vehicles] as a point of comparison to reveal the perfectly consummate three tracks of the nature of mind;
now, setting aside the three teachings, it directly elucidates the nature of mind.
When the true nature-principle (*dharmatā-naya*) is conjoined with actual wisdom,
it is called "that which can reach.
Because it is able to give rise to function from within principle, it is said that "principle is superior to phenomena."
Question:
True nature is inherently conjoined with ultimate wisdom;
what concern does it have with external objects that you say the mutual entry of large and small forms results from accords with principle?
Answer: However, this nature of directness pervades the entire dharma-realm;
those who are deluded perceive it as internal and external, while those who have awakened realize it is but the single mind.
Therefore, while the four eyes and two wisdoms perceive the myriad phenomena in their dense array,
the Buddha-eye and the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñā) are the profound stillness of true emptiness.
Although this is but an initial contemplation, how could it allow one to follow delusion?
To restrain the mind so that it follows principle is none other than the nature of the mind.
Regarding the subsequent question:
does each individual causal mind possess the causes for all ten realms?
Furthermore, does each individual realm-fruit possess the fruits of all ten realms?
In the response, the initial general answer states that they "all mutually exist," which is so by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).
The principle that a single thought-moment as cause possesses all ten [realms] is such that how could the fruit of a single realm possibly belong to only one realm?
Nevertheless, it is said that a single fruit possesses all ten fruits.
Since the fruit is separated [from its causes] and appears to manifest universally, it may seem difficult [to understand];
however, if one knows that within the ten [causes], each single mind necessarily pervades all ten as they arise accordingly,
then a single fruit is endowed with all ten causes.
One cause possesses ten causes;
therefore, it is said that because the principle of the causes is pervasive, they are easy to understand.
In this text, the pervasiveness of the causes is first clarified.
Next, the separation of the result is explained.
Regarding the initial cause, which is pervasive, only the beginning and the end are mentioned;
the intermediate stages are to be known by inference.
Regarding the maiden Maitrakanyā:
as stated in the *Cittaviveka-śāstra*,
the elder Maitrakanyā desired to accompany [his caravan] into the ocean to gather treasures.
He asked his mother for permission to depart.
His mother said, "I have only you; why would you abandon me and leave?"
The mother, fearing he would depart, then embraced his feet;
the young girl then seized her mother’s hair with her hand,
and a single strand of hair fell out.
The mother then released him.
Upon reaching the island in the sea, he saw a glowing iron wheel descending from the sky and alighting upon the crown of his head.
He then made this vow:
"May the sufferings of the entire dharma realm all gather within my own body.
By the power of this vow, the wheel of fire finally fell.
From this point on, upon casting off his life, he was reborn in the sixth heaven;
yet, by disobeying his mother and damaging her hair, he formed a hellish mind.
By then giving rise to a great vow, he immediately entered the realm of the Buddhas.
To disparage those who have not yet received a prediction of enlightenment while praising those who have already received it—
though they have not yet received the prediction, they already belong to the Buddha’s mind;
yet by disparaging those who have received the prediction, one creates the realm of hell.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Contemplating Emptiness and Non-Realization" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"I have realized non-retrogression, while others will never attain it," and thus he treats others with contempt and mockery.
Because of this matter, one becomes distant from awakening and far removed from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
If one repents in this very life, after a long time one will again rely upon the *prajñāpāramitā*; however, if one does not repent immediately, [the consequence is otherwise].
One should know that this offense is weightier than the four prohibitions and more grave than the five heinous crimes.
One should know that such a person is a *caṇḍāla* among bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, by citing what follows below, the text briefly clarifies the separation from the fruit and demonstrates the characteristics of its difficulty to manifest.
According to the discourse on the principle of phenomena,
each of the fruits of the ten realms possesses its own ten fruits; therefore,
it is said that both ordinary beings and sages alike possess the five aggregates.
The aggregates (skandhas) are themselves the fruit.
"Ordinary beings" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings, while "sages" refers to the four classes of noble ones.
Although each possesses [these aggregates], they are distinct.
The aggregates of an arhat cannot be like the aggregates of an ordinary person.
Regarding the statement "cannot," the intended meaning is that the aggregates of an ordinary person are not the same as the aggregates of an arhat.
Furthermore, the Buddha is fully endowed with [all realms]; taking one instance, the fruit of Buddhahood is complete within the ten realms.
However, one cannot equate the aggregates (skandhas) of a Sage with those of an ordinary being;
rather, it is simply that the fruit of Buddhahood is capable of encompassing the ten realms.
Ultimately, one must not take the Buddha’s realm of hell to be the realm of hell for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
This is spoken from the perspective of one who has already perfected the fruit of Buddhahood and acts accordingly.
The ten realms are already complete.
From the first stage (bhūmi) to the first dwelling (vihāra), they are partially complete;
even in ordinary beings, they are complete as the fundamental principle (li).
Thus, each individual realm-fruit possesses its own ten [factors] without mutual confusion;
this is the approach taken for the sake of ease.
Furthermore, regarding the statements that "the causes interpenetrate" and "the realms are separated," from the perspective of principle,
a single moment of causal mind actually possesses the causes and effects of the ten realms and the hundred realms.
Why is this? It is like clouds arising: when a single dharma-realm mind arises, it immediately possesses the ten realms and the ten suchnesses.
These ten suchnesses are nothing other than the dharmas of cause and effect.
One should know that the conditions of mutual interaction belong to the cause,
while the retribution belongs to the fruit;
thus, in every single thought-moment, one constantly possesses the causes and fruits of the ten realms, both the environment and its inhabitants.
Therefore, the *Buddhagotra-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha perceives that within the minds of all sentient beings,
there is a Tathāgata sitting cross-legged."
It still possesses the fruit of Buddhahood;
the same applies to the other fruits.
Therefore, although the lower stages possess both cause and fruit, [they do not constitute the ultimate].
However, this is based on rationality;
therefore, the expression "separated by a result" arises.
As for the subsequent question:

If one follows the previous answer, the reason is clear and easy to understand.

It is simply that one is deluded regarding the fact that the One Mind possesses all phenomena.
